stem: A medication error reaches a client, but immediate assessment shows no apparent injury. Which nursing response best supports patient safety?

options.A: Assess the client, follow required clinical and organizational incident-reporting processes, document the client's assessment and care factually, and continue indicated monitoring.
options.B: Withhold reporting unless the client later develops an injury or measurable adverse effect from the error.
options.C: Complete the causal investigation independently before informing the care team or using the organization's safety-reporting process.
options.D: Continue routine observation and delay formal event reporting unless symptoms or injury emerge.

rationale: The 2026 NCSBN test plan includes identifying situations where incident/event reporting is appropriate, acknowledging and documenting practice errors and near misses, evaluating the response to an error/event, and escalating unsafe practice when indicated. A no-apparent-harm outcome does not erase the need to assess the client and follow required reporting processes. Clinical documentation should remain a factual record of the client's condition, assessment, interventions, and response; the organization's separate safety-reporting process is followed according to policy.
educational_objective: After a medication error reaches a client, assess and monitor the client and complete required clinical and safety reporting even when no immediate injury is apparent.
source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_locator: Appendix A, printed p. 25, Safety and Infection Prevention and Control → Reporting of Incident/Event/Irregular Occurrence/Variance: identify when reporting is appropriate; acknowledge/document practice errors and near misses; evaluate response to error/event/occurrence.
source_claim_supported: NCSBN explicitly includes reporting of incidents/events, acknowledging and documenting practice errors/near misses, and evaluating the client's response to an error/event under Safety and Infection Prevention and Control.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Same Appendix A, printed p. 25, Reporting of Incident/Event/Irregular Occurrence/Variance.
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Reporting of Incident/Event/Irregular Occurrence/Variance

source_original.stem: A medication error reaches a client, but immediate assessment shows no apparent injury. Which nursing response best supports patient safety?

options.A: Assess the client, use required clinical and safety reporting channels, document factual care, and continue indicated monitoring.
options.B: Withhold reporting unless the client later develops an injury or measurable adverse effect from the error.
options.C: Complete the causal investigation independently before informing the care team or the organization’s safety process.
options.D: Document routine medication administration and continue observation; formal event reporting can wait unless symptoms or injury emerge.

source_original.rationale: The 2026 NCSBN test plan includes acknowledging and documenting practice errors and near misses, reporting incidents/events, intervening or escalating safety concerns, and evaluating the client’s response. A no-harm outcome does not eliminate the need for assessment and required reporting.
source_original.source_detail: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — ‘Reporting of Incident/Event’ and practice-error/near-miss activities: acknowledge/document errors, report incidents, and evaluate client response. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; Reporting of Incident/Event and infection/safety activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the key and no-harm error construct. Clarified the distinction between factual clinical documentation and the organization's separate incident-reporting process, avoiding the unsupported implication that a specific report form or channel is universal.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Medication error — client assessment and incident reporting
audit_findings.source_authority: Current official NCSBN 2026 Test Plan, appropriate for NCLEX safety/reporting construct.
audit_findings.exact_locator: Appendix A printed p.25, Reporting of Incident/Event/Irregular Occurrence/Variance.
audit_findings.claim_audit: No claim that a specific form, notification order, or charting phrase is universally mandated.

distractor_audit.A: Only option addressing client assessment, required reporting, factual care documentation, and monitoring.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because absence of current harm does not negate reporting of an error that reached the client.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because reporting/clinical response should not wait for an independent causal investigation.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because reporting is not contingent on later symptoms/injury.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A aligns with the complete NCSBN safety-response construct.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are realistic post-error actions.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Confirmed the final item does not conflate the safety report with the medical record and does not invent universal disclosure mechanics.
